identity.title: Breaking the Performance Ceiling in Reinforcement Learning requires Inference Strategies

problem.claim: Complex multi-agent reinforcement-learning problems can exceed the capabilities of converged systems during zero-shot execution.

gap.claim: The abstract identifies a need to understand whether execution-time inference phases and inference-strategy choices can overcome this performance ceiling.

contributions.claim: An execution-time inference phase with a corresponding inference strategy for complex multi-agent RL.
A large evaluation of inference strategies across 17 tasks, using additional execution-time wall-clock budget.
Release of the experimental data and code.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors present execution-time inference and inference-strategy selection as key to breaking performance ceilings in complex multi-agent RL, and describe their study as the largest on inference strategies for complex RL to date.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report improvements of up to 126% and 45% on average over the previous state of the art across 17 tasks, using only a couple of extra seconds of execution-time wall-clock time.
The authors report promising compute-scaling properties, supported by more than 60,000 experiments.

narrative_sequence.summary: Real-world RL applications are described as difficult, combinatorial, and coordination-intensive.
Even converged state-of-the-art systems may hit a ceiling that zero-shot inference cannot overcome.
The work uses an execution-time inference phase that explores multiple attempts within a time and compute budget, with strategy choice treated as consequential.
The authors report substantial gains across 17 tasks, scaling behavior, and release of data and code.

source_observation.claim: The abstract links a specific execution-time budget and inference-strategy choice to reported gains over zero-shot execution and prior state of the art.

lessons.interpretation: A paper can make a stronger systems argument by treating inference-time computation as an explicit controllable resource rather than evaluating only fixed-policy execution.
lessons.application: When a learned system faces a deployment-time ceiling, define an inference budget, compare multiple execution strategies under that budget, and report gains against the fixed or zero-shot baseline.
lessons.exception: This framing is unsuitable when deployment forbids extra latency or computation, or when the task has no meaningful opportunity for multiple candidate attempts.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the inference strategies, task identities, evaluation metric, baseline implementation, or statistical variability.
The meanings of the reported percentage improvements and the conditions behind the compute-scaling results are unspecified.
